A Philippine employment contract selects State X law. Employer E invokes that law to justify dismissal but submits only counsel's English quotation from an untranslated, unauthenticated website. Corporate rights over public and private land

P Corp. is organized under Philippine law and satisfies the constitutional sixty-percent Filipino ownership requirement. It asks the State for a patent conveying ownership of six hundred hectares of alienable public agricultural land; alternatively, it seeks a twenty-five-year lease of the same tract. The patent is constitutionally barred. A private corporation may not own alienable land of the public domain, even when it satisfies the Filipino-ownership threshold, and may hold such land only by lease. The proposed six-hundred-hectare, twenty-five-year public-land lease is within Article XII, Section 3’s maximum area and original term, but remains subject to the Public Land Act, award procedures, and other statutory conditions; renewal may not exceed one additional twenty-five-year period. The Philippines ratifies a Senate-concurred treaty requiring an act that the Constitution expressly forbids.
